solution:
The first matrix is of order \(3 \times 1\) and the second of order \(1 \times 3\), so the product is of order \(3 \times 3\). Each entry is (row entry) \(\times\) (column entry).
Row 1 uses \(3\): \(3(2),\ 3(-4),\ 3(3) = 6,\ -12,\ 9\).
Row 2 uses \(2\): \(4,\ -8,\ 6\). Row 3 uses \(1\): \(2,\ -4,\ 3\).
\(\therefore \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -4 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -12 & 9 \\ 4 & -8 & 6 \\ 2 & -4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)

Here a \(1 \times 3\) matrix multiplies a \(3 \times 1\) matrix, so the product is \(1 \times 1\).
The single entry is \(2(4) + (-1)(3) + 3(1) = 8 - 3 + 3 = 8\).
\(\therefore \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 - 9 & 1 + 6 \\ 16 + 6 & 4 - 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 7 \\ 22 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(BA = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 + 4 & -12 + 2 \\ 3 - 8 & -9 - 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -10 \\ -5 & -13 \end{bmatrix}\)
The corresponding entries differ (for instance \((1,1)\): \(-5 \ne 8\)).
\(\therefore AB \ne BA\)

\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 13 & 2 & 14 \\ -6 & 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\)
(e.g. entry \((1,1) = -1(2) + 1(3) + 1(1) = 2\).)
\(BA = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -7 & 6 \\ -1 & -3 & 5 \\ 4 & 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\)
The two products are not equal (entry \((1,1)\): \(2 \ne 4\)); matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.
\(\therefore AB \ne BA\)

Take the rotation matrices \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\phi & -\sin\phi \\ \sin\phi & \cos\phi \end{bmatrix}\).
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta\cos\phi - \sin\theta\sin\phi & -\cos\theta\sin\phi - \sin\theta\cos\phi \\ \sin\theta\cos\phi + \cos\theta\sin\phi & -\sin\theta\sin\phi + \cos\theta\cos\phi \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta+\phi) & -\sin(\theta+\phi) \\ \sin(\theta+\phi) & \cos(\theta+\phi) \end{bmatrix}\)
Interchanging \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) gives \(BA = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\phi+\theta) & -\sin(\phi+\theta) \\ \sin(\phi+\theta) & \cos(\phi+\theta) \end{bmatrix}\), and \(\theta + \phi = \phi + \theta\).
\(\therefore AB = BA = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta+\phi) & -\sin(\theta+\phi) \\ \sin(\theta+\phi) & \cos(\theta+\phi) \end{bmatrix}\)
_note: The printed A carries BOTH sines positive, \(\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\), while B correctly carries \(-\sin\phi\). With A as printed the claim is FALSE: e.g. the \((1,2)\) entry of AB is \(-\cos\theta\sin\phi + \sin\theta\cos\phi = \sin(\theta-\phi)\) whereas that of BA is \(\cos\phi\sin\theta - \sin\phi\cos\theta\)... in fact the \((1,1)\) entries already differ: \(\cos\theta\cos\phi + \sin\theta\sin\phi\) vs \(\cos\phi\cos\theta - \sin\phi\sin\theta\). Solved for the intended rotation form \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\), which is the form the same book prints in Q.23 and in Ex 4.7 Q.14. The book prints no key for this item.

solution:
\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 8 \\ -2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 8 \\ -2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(= \begin{bmatrix} 16 - 16 & 32 - 32 \\ -8 + 8 & -16 + 16 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\therefore A^{2} = O\), the null matrix of order 2.

\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -4 & 19 \end{bmatrix}\), so
\((AB)C = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -4 & 19 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 4 & -4 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 26 & -8 & -34 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(BC = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 \\ 6 & 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix}\), so
\(A(BC) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 \\ 6 & 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 4 & -4 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 26 & -8 & -34 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore A(BC) = (AB)C = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 4 & -4 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 26 & -8 & -34 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 3 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 13 & 11 \\ 5 & 13 \end{bmatrix}\), so
\((AB)C = \begin{bmatrix} 13 & 11 \\ 5 & 13 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 50 & 46 \\ 28 & 44 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(BC = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 3 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -4 \\ 12 & 12 \\ -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), so
\(A(BC) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -4 \\ 12 & 12 \\ -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 50 & 46 \\ 28 & 44 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore A(BC) = (AB)C = \begin{bmatrix} 50 & 46 \\ 28 & 44 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(B + C = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 5 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\), so
\(A(B+C) = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 5 & -3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 12 - 10 & 8 + 6 \\ 6 + 15 & 4 - 9 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 14 \\ 21 & -5 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} -10 & 8 \\ 7 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(AC = \begin{bmatrix} 12 & 6 \\ 14 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(AB + AC = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 14 \\ 21 & -5 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore A(B+C) = AB + AC = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 14 \\ 21 & -5 \end{bmatrix}\)
_note: The shared instruction prints \(A(B+C) = AB + BC\); the distributive law is \(A(B+C) = AB + AC\). Verified for the correct statement. As printed the claim is false here: \(BC = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & -2 \\ 8 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(AB + BC = \begin{bmatrix} -12 & 6 \\ 15 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \ne A(B+C)\). The book prints no key for this item.

solution:
\(B + C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 4 & -3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ -4 & 3 \\ 8 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), so
\(A(B+C) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ -4 & 3 \\ 8 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 4 + 24 & 2 - 3 + 0 \\ 4 - 12 + 16 & 4 + 9 + 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 30 & -1 \\ 8 & 13 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 6 \\ 4 & 15 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(AC = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & -7 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(AB + AC = \begin{bmatrix} 30 & -1 \\ 8 & 13 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore A(B+C) = AB + AC = \begin{bmatrix} 30 & -1 \\ 8 & 13 \end{bmatrix}\)
_note: The shared instruction prints \(A(B+C) = AB + BC\); the distributive law is \(A(B+C) = AB + AC\). Here the printed right-hand side is not merely wrong but undefined: B and C are both \(3 \times 2\), so the product BC does not exist. Verified for the correct statement. The book prints no key for this item.

solution:
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 3 & 7 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 - 6 & -1 - 14 \\ 15 + 18 & -5 + 42 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & -15 \\ 33 & 37 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(2I = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\therefore AB - 2I = \begin{bmatrix} -3 - 2 & -15 - 0 \\ 33 - 0 & 37 - 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & -15 \\ 33 & 35 \end{bmatrix}\)

A is \(2 \times 3\) and B is \(3 \times 2\), so AB is a square matrix of order 2.
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 - 3 + 2 & 8 + 0 - 4 \\ -1 - 2 + 0 & -2 + 0 - 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ -3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(|AB| = 3(-2) - 4(-3) = -6 + 12 = 6 \ne 0\).
\(\therefore\) AB is a non-singular matrix.

\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \alpha & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha^{2} & 0 \\ \alpha + 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)
Equating with \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\): \(\alpha^{2} = 1\) and \(\alpha + 1 = 2\).
The second gives \(\alpha = 1\), which also satisfies \(\alpha^{2} = 1\) (the other root \(\alpha = -1\) fails it).
\(\therefore \alpha = 1\)

\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 8 & 8 \\ 8 & 9 & 8 \\ 8 & 8 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\)
(e.g. entry \((1,1) = 1 + 4 + 4 = 9\), entry \((1,2) = 2 + 2 + 4 = 8\).)
\(4A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 8 & 8 \\ 8 & 4 & 8 \\ 8 & 8 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^{2} - 4A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = 5I\).
Every off-diagonal entry is 0 and all diagonal entries are equal.
\(\therefore A^{2} - 4A\) is a scalar matrix, namely \(5I\).

\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 7 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 - 7 & 49 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -8 & 49 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(A^{2} - 8A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -8 & 49 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 0 \\ -8 & 56 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 \end{bmatrix}\)
So \(A^{2} - 8A - kI = O\) gives \(\begin{bmatrix} -7 - k & 0 \\ 0 & -7 - k \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore k = -7\)

\(A + B = \begin{bmatrix} 13 & 0 \\ 20 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\), so \((A+B)^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 13 & 0 \\ 20 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 13 & 0 \\ 20 & -3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 169 & 0 \\ 200 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\).
Next \(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 104 & 52 \\ 130 & 65 \end{bmatrix}\), \(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 80 & -64 \\ 100 & -80 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} -15 & 12 \\ -30 & 24 \end{bmatrix}\).
Adding, \(A^{2} + AB + B^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 104 + 80 - 15 & 52 - 64 + 12 \\ 130 + 100 - 30 & 65 - 80 + 24 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 169 & 0 \\ 200 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\).
(The identity holds here because \(BA = \begin{bmatrix} 40 - 40 & 20 - 20 \\ 80 - 80 & 40 - 40 \end{bmatrix} = O\), and \((A+B)^{2} = A^{2} + AB + BA + B^{2}\).)
\(\therefore (A+B)^{2} = A^{2} + AB + B^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 169 & 0 \\ 200 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 - 1 & 3 + 2 \\ -3 - 2 & -1 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 5 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(5A = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 5 \\ -5 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\), \(7I = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(A^{2} - 5A + 7I = \begin{bmatrix} 8 - 15 + 7 & 5 - 5 + 0 \\ -5 + 5 + 0 & 3 - 10 + 7 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\therefore A^{2} - 5A + 7I = O\)

\(A + B = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 5 \\ -5 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), \(A - B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), so
\((A+B)(A-B) = \begin{bmatrix} 5 - 15 & 15 + 5 \\ -5 - 15 & -15 + 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -10 & 20 \\ -20 & -10 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 24 \\ -24 & -7 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ -4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^{2} - B^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} -10 & 20 \\ -20 & -10 \end{bmatrix}\).
(This works because these particular matrices commute: \(AB = BA = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 11 \\ -11 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).)
\(\therefore (A+B)(A-B) = A^{2} - B^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} -10 & 20 \\ -20 & -10 \end{bmatrix}\)

\((A+B)^{2} = A^{2} + AB + BA + B^{2}\), so the given condition reduces to \(AB + BA = O\).
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & a \\ -1 & b \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & a + 2b \\ 0 & -(a + 2b) \end{bmatrix}\)
\(BA = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & a \\ -1 & b \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 - a & 4 - 2a \\ -1 - b & -2 - 2b \end{bmatrix}\)
Equating \(AB + BA\) to the null matrix: \(2 - a = 0\) and \(-1 - b = 0\), giving \(a = 2\), \(b = -1\); these also satisfy the remaining two entries, since \(a + 2b = 0\).
\(\therefore a = 2,\ b = -1\)

A is \(2 \times 2\) and B is \(2 \times 1\), so X is \(2 \times 1\); let \(X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}\).
\(AX = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x - 2y \\ -2x + y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\)
So \(x - 2y = -3\) and \(-2x + y = -1\). Multiplying the first by 2 and adding: \(-3y = -7\), so \(y = \frac{7}{3}\), and then \(x = 2\left(\frac{7}{3}\right) - 3 = \frac{5}{3}\).
\(\therefore X = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{5}{3} \\ \frac{7}{3} \end{bmatrix}\)

\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 - 8 & -6 + 4 \\ 12 - 8 & -8 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 4 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(kA - 2I = \begin{bmatrix} 3k - 2 & -2k \\ 4k & -2k - 2 \end{bmatrix}\)
Equating corresponding entries: \(3k - 2 = 1\) gives \(k = 1\), and \(k = 1\) also satisfies \(-2k = -2\), \(4k = 4\), \(-2k - 2 = -4\).
\(\therefore k = 1\)

First multiply the left two matrices:
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & x & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 3 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 + 4x & 4 + 5x & 8 + 6x \end{bmatrix}\)
Now multiply by the column matrix:
\((4 + 4x)(1) + (4 + 5x)(-2) + (8 + 6x)(3) = 4 + 4x - 8 - 10x + 24 + 18x = 20 + 12x\)
Setting this equal to 0: \(12x = -20\).
\(\therefore x = -\frac{5}{3}\)

\(4\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -3 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 - 3 & -4 + 3 & 12 - 4 \\ 4 - 2 & 0 - 1 & 8 - 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -1 & 8 \\ 2 & -1 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -1 & 8 \\ 2 & -1 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 + 1 + 8 \\ 4 + 1 + 7 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 19 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix}\)
Equating with \(\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}\):
\(\therefore x = 19,\ y = 12\)

\(3\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - 4\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 - 4 & 0 - 4 \\ 0 + 4 & 6 - 8 \\ 6 - 12 & 6 - 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -6 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -6 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 - 8 \\ 4 - 4 \\ -6 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -6 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}\)
Equating with \(\begin{bmatrix} x - 3 \\ y - 1 \\ 2z \end{bmatrix}\): \(x - 3 = -6\), \(y - 1 = 0\), \(2z = -2\).
\(\therefore x = -3,\ y = 1,\ z = -1\)

\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\alpha & \sin\alpha \\ -\sin\alpha & \cos\alpha \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \cos\alpha & \sin\alpha \\ -\sin\alpha & \cos\alpha \end{bmatrix}\)
\(= \begin{bmatrix} \cos^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\alpha & \cos\alpha\sin\alpha + \sin\alpha\cos\alpha \\ -\sin\alpha\cos\alpha - \cos\alpha\sin\alpha & -\sin^{2}\alpha + \cos^{2}\alpha \end{bmatrix}\)
Using \(\cos^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\alpha = \cos 2\alpha\) and \(2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha = \sin 2\alpha\):
\(\therefore A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos 2\alpha & \sin 2\alpha \\ -\sin 2\alpha & \cos 2\alpha \end{bmatrix}\)

\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 10 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\), \(BA = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 12 & 20 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\).
The corresponding entries differ, so \(AB \ne BA\).
Now \(|AB| = 4(7) - 2(10) = 8\), while \(|A| = 5 - 6 = -1\) and \(|B| = 0 - 8 = -8\), so \(|A| \cdot |B| = (-1)(-8) = 8\).
\(\therefore AB \ne BA\), but \(|AB| = |A| \cdot |B| = 8\)

Write the quantities as a \(2 \times 2\) matrix (rows: Jay, Ram; columns: pens, notebooks) and the prices as a column matrix.
\(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 8 \\ 5 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 24 + 80 \\ 30 + 120 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 104 \\ 150 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\therefore\) Jay requires Rs. 104 and Ram requires Rs. 150.
